newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ATHLETICS-CHRISTIE HAS NO REGRETS OVER RETIREMENT.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-CHRISTIE HAS NO REGRETS OVER RETIREMENT.

text.p: Linford Christie said on Tuesday that he was not excited about running anymore and confirmed his retirement as well as his desire to pursue his coaching career.
Christie announced his retirement -- not for the first time -- on Saturday and said on Tuesday he was happy with the decision.
"I've always said that when I would wake up one morning and not feel like competing, then that would be the time to stop," he said.
"It would have been nice to give the fans one more meeting but you've got to quit sometime.
"That's it, I will not change my mind."
The 37-year-old Briton, who attended the recently-ended Athens world championships as a television analyst, said he had not felt frustrated by not being on the track.
"Watching the 100 and the 200 metres I did not hear the pounding of my heart I usually have when I'm not out there," he said.
Christie will now concentrate on coaching several leading athletes including Namibian Frankie Fredericks, Jamaican Merlene Ottey and Briton Jamie Baulch.
"I've been in the sport since 1979, I've learned a lot and I feel I can pass it on," he said.
The greatest European sprinter in history, Christie made a late start to his international career, reaching his peak with gold in the 1992 Olympics and the 1993 world championships.

Christie collected 23 medals, including 10 golds from major championships, but his reign at the top came to an incongruous end when he was disqualified from the 100 metres final in last year's Olympics for two false starts.

In Athens he witnessed the start of the new era with titles in the 100 and 200 metres respectively for American Maurice Greene and Trinidad's Ato Boldon, both aged 23 -- 14 years younger than Christie.
Christie said he was slightly irritated to hear them keep talking about crushing the world record.
"They should not say that they are going to do it," he said. "They should just go out there and surprise everybody by doing it."
But he said he did hope the record of 9.84 seconds set by Canadian Donovan Bailey last year in Atlanta would fall.
"It would be good for the sport, it would take it to another level," he said, before naming Boldon as the type of character that athletics needed to attract attention.
"It's good to have somebody like Boldon around because he's such a great personality," he said.
